text: Johnson refuses to make his own admiration the measure of the work; for such admiration might be no more than the taste of one age and of one temper. His question is what time has done with it. The writer whose credit is upheld by the fashion of his day, by local customs, or by the contests of a party, may be applauded while that fashion subsists; when it is gone, the applause which it supported goes with it. That work alone has made good its claim which still pleases readers who inherit none of the circumstances of its first audience. They come without partiality to the trial; they have neither friendship for the author nor interest in his opinions, and read him because he yet gives pleasure.
